config.title: Specificity

intro.title: Specificity
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage to learn how CSS specificity determines which styles are applied when multiple rules target the same element. You will explore the core concept of specificity by writing CSS rules with different selectors, such as element, class, and ID selectors, to see which one takes precedence. The main technologies involved are CSS selectors and the specificity calculation rules. By the end, you will understand how to predict and control style conflicts in your web projects.
intro.usecase: CSS specificity is crucial for maintaining consistent and predictable styling in complex web applications. For example, in a dashboard with multiple widgets, you might have a general rule setting all text to black, but need a specific widget's header to be blue. Without understanding specificity, your blue header rule could be overridden by a more general or later rule, causing visual bugs. Developers use specificity daily when styling interactive components like navigation menus, form inputs, or modals to ensure the correct styles apply, especially when using component libraries or overriding third-party CSS.

objectives: Apply CSS specificity rules to override conflicting styles
Construct selector combinations with different specificity weights
Manipulate the cascade by adjusting selector specificity
Implement the !important declaration to control style precedence
Configure CSS rules to achieve intended visual outcomes through specificity management
Update existing stylesheets by modifying selector specificity
Integrate specificity calculations to resolve style conflicts in practical scenarios

steps.title: Create a basic HTML structure to style
steps.instruction: Create a simple HTML file with a heading, paragraph, and button that will be targeted by CSS rules.
steps.hint: Use standard HTML elements like h1, p, and button. You can add placeholder text content.
steps.analogousExample:
Welcome to CSS Specificity

This paragraph will be styled with CSS.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>CSS Specificity Practice</title>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add your HTML elements here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: A basic HTML structure with at least three different elements (heading, paragraph, button) that can be targeted with CSS rules.
successCriteria: The HTML file contains h1, p, and button elements with some text content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have some HTML elements, but make sure you include at least a heading (h1), paragraph (p), and button element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please create a basic HTML file with h1, p, and button elements inside the body.

steps.title: Add a class selector to style an element
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule that uses a class selector to apply basic styling to an element. Create a class named 'highlight' that sets the background color to yellow and adds padding of 10px.
steps.hint: In CSS, class selectors start with a dot (.) followed by the class name. Define the rule in a style tag or external stylesheet.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>CSS Specificity Practice</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your CSS class selector here */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add your HTML elements here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS rule with class selector '.highlight' is created, applying yellow background and 10px padding.
successCriteria: The CSS contains a class selector named 'highlight' with properties for background-color and padding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your class selector includes both background-color and padding properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule is missing or incorrect. Remember to use a dot (.) before the class name and define the specified properties.

steps.title: Add an element selector with conflicting style
steps.instruction: In the style tag, add a CSS rule using an element selector that targets the same element as your class selector, but with a different color property value to create a conflict.
steps.hint: Use an element selector like 'p' or 'div' and set a different 'color' property value than your class selector uses.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>CSS Specificity Practice</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your CSS class selector here */
        
        /* Add your element selector with conflicting style here */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add your HTML elements here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have two CSS rules targeting the same element with different color values - one using a class selector and one using an element selector.
successCriteria: An element selector CSS rule is added with a different color property value than the class selector
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an element selector, but make sure it has a different color value than your class selector to create a clear conflict.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a CSS rule using an element selector (like 'p' or 'div') with a different color property value than your class selector uses.

steps.title: Add an ID selector with higher specificity
steps.instruction: Inside the <style> block, add a CSS rule using an ID selector that sets the color of the element to 'red'. This will demonstrate how ID selectors have higher specificity than class and element selectors.
steps.hint: Use the syntax '#yourId { color: red; }' where 'yourId' is the ID you want to target. Remember that ID selectors start with a '#' symbol.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>CSS Specificity Practice</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your CSS class selector here */
        
        /* Add your element selector with conflicting style here */
        
        /* Add your ID selector with higher specificity here */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add your HTML elements here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS rule using an ID selector is added to the style block, which will override styles from class and element selectors due to its higher specificity.
successCriteria: The CSS rule includes an ID selector (starting with '#') and sets the 'color' property to 'red'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a CSS rule, but it might not be using an ID selector or setting the color to red. Remember to use the '#' symbol for ID selectors and set 'color: red;'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule is missing or incorrect. Make sure you're using an ID selector (starting with '#') and setting the color property to 'red'.

steps.title: Add inline styles to demonstrate highest specificity
steps.instruction: Add an inline style attribute to the element in your HTML to set its color to 'purple' and override all other CSS rules.
steps.hint: Inline styles are added directly to an HTML element using the style attribute, like style="color: purple;".
steps.analogousExample: This text is purple due to inline style.
steps.seedCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>CSS Specificity Practice</title>
    <style>
        /* Add your CSS class selector here */
        
        /* Add your element selector with conflicting style here */
        
        /* Add your ID selector with higher specificity here */
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <!-- Add your HTML elements here -->
</body>
</html>
steps.expectedOutcome: The element will have an inline style attribute that sets its color to purple, demonstrating the highest specificity level.
successCriteria: An inline style attribute with color: purple; is added to an HTML element in the body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an inline style, but make sure it sets the color to 'purple' to clearly demonstrate the override.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inline styles are added directly to HTML elements using the style attribute. Try adding style="color: purple;" to an element.

steps.title: Use the !important declaration
steps.instruction: Add the !important declaration to the class selector's color property to override the inline style.
steps.hint: Place !important right before the semicolon in the color property of the class selector.
steps.seedCode: This is a paragraph with multiple conflicting styles.
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph text will turn green because the !important declaration on the class selector overrides the inline style.
successCriteria: The class selector's color property includes !important before the semicolon.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you added !important to the color property in the class selector, right before the semicolon.
steps.feedbackWrong: The !important declaration wasn't added correctly. Check that you placed it in the class selector's color property.

steps.title: Create a more specific selector combination
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule that combines an element selector with a class selector (e.g., p.my-class) to create a selector with higher specificity than the individual class selector.
steps.hint:
Write a selector that targets

elements with the class 'my-class'. Place it after the existing ID selector rule in the
steps.seedCode: This is a paragraph with multiple conflicting styles.
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph text will turn blue because the p.my-class selector has higher specificity than .my-class but lower than #my-id and inline styles.
successCriteria: A CSS rule with selector 'p.my-class' is added to the <style> section, setting the color property to blue.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the exact selector 'p.my-class' (element followed immediately by class without space) and setting the color to blue.
steps.feedbackWrong: The combined selector wasn't added correctly. Remember to write 'p.my-class' as the selector and set 'color: blue;' inside the rule.

steps.title: Add nested elements to demonstrate inheritance
steps.instruction: Add a nested span element inside the existing paragraph to demonstrate how specificity interacts with inheritance.
steps.hint: Inside the paragraph, add a span element with some text content. You can place it before or after the existing text.
steps.analogousExample:
/* Example: adding a nested element */

This is a paragraph with a nested span inside.
steps.seedCode: This is a paragraph with multiple conflicting styles.
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph now contains a nested span element, setting up the structure to explore inheritance in the next steps.
successCriteria: A span element is nested inside the existing paragraph element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the span element is properly nested inside the paragraph element and contains some text content.
steps.feedbackWrong: The span element is not properly nested inside the paragraph. Check your HTML structure to ensure the span is a child of the p element.

steps.title: Create a specificity conflict with pseudo-classes
steps.instruction: Add a pseudo-class selector for the paragraph element to create a hover effect with a different color.
steps.hint: Use the :hover pseudo-class on the p selector to specify a color that conflicts with the existing styles.
steps.seedCode: This is a paragraph with multiple conflicting styles.
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph will have a hover effect with a new color, adding another layer to the specificity conflict.
successCriteria: A :hover pseudo-class selector is added to the p element with a color property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've added a :hover pseudo-class selector for the p element with a color property.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction: you need to add a pseudo-class selector (like :hover) to the paragraph element with a color property.

steps.title: Review and test all specificity scenarios
steps.instruction: Add a combined element.class selector that targets paragraphs with the 'my-class' class and sets their color to blue to demonstrate higher specificity than element selectors alone.
steps.hint: Write a CSS selector that combines the element name 'p' with the class selector '.my-class' using no space between them.
steps.seedCode: This is a paragraph with multiple conflicting styles.
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph text will appear orange (inline style) because inline styles have the highest specificity, but the combined selector demonstrates how element.class selectors have higher specificity than element or class selectors alone.
successCriteria: A combined selector 'p.my-class' is added with 'color: blue;' to demonstrate specificity hierarchy.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the combined selector 'p.my-class' with the color property set to blue. The selector should have no space between 'p' and '.my-class'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The combined selector wasn't added correctly. Remember to create a selector that targets paragraphs with the 'my-class' class using 'p.my-class' and set the color to blue.
